title: Applying a Moving Heatload in ANSYS
text:
Applying a Moving Heatload to a Surface in ANSYS Mechanical
Often times when analysing a moving load, it becomes extremely tedious to move said load manually. This code allows for the process to be automated as shown below:



A heat load moving in a circular manner on a flat plate


Note: the logic behind the element face selection process can be found here
import numpy as np

eTypeToFaceIndex = {
    ElementTypeEnum.kTri3 : [ [ 0, 1, 2 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTri6 : [ [ 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kQuad4 : [ [ 0, 1, 2, 4 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kQuad8 : [ [ 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTet4 : [ [ 0, 1, 3 ], [ 1, 2, 3 ], [ 2, 0, 3 ], [ 0, 2, 1 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTet10 : [ [ 0, 1, 3, 4, 8, 7 ], [ 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 8 ], [ 2, 0, 3, 6, 7, 9 ], [ 0, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kPyramid5 : [ [ 0, 3, 2, 1 ], [ 0, 1, 4 ], [ 1, 2, 4 ], [ 3, 4, 2 ], [ 0, 4, 3 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kPyramid13 : [ [ 0, 3, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6, 5 ], [ 0, 1, 4, 5, 10, 9 ], [ 1, 2, 4, 6, 11, 10 ], [ 3, 4, 2, 12, 11, 7 ], [ 0, 4, 3, 9, 12, 8 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kWedge6 : [ [ 0, 2, 1 ], [ 3, 4, 5 ], [ 0, 1, 4, 3 ], [ 1, 2, 5, 4 ], [ 0, 3, 5, 2 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kWedge15 : [ [ 0, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6 ], [ 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11 ], [ 0, 1, 4, 3, 6, 13, 9, 12 ], [ 1, 2, 5, 4, 7, 14, 10, 13 ], [ 0, 3, 5, 2, 12, 11, 14, 8 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kHex8 : [ [ 0, 1, 5, 4 ], [ 1, 2, 6, 5 ], [ 2, 3, 7, 6 ], [ 3, 0, 4, 7 ], [ 0, 3, 2, 1 ], [ 4, 5, 6, 7 ] ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kHex20 : [ [ 0, 1, 5, 4, 8, 17, 12, 16 ], [ 1, 2, 6, 5, 9, 18, 13, 17 ], [ 2, 3, 7, 6, 10, 19, 14, 18 ], [ 3, 0, 4, 7, 11, 16, 15, 19 ], [ 0, 3, 2, 1, 11, 10, 9, 8 ], [ 4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15 ] ]
}

axeDict = {"xy": [0, 1], "xz": [0, 2], "yz": [1, 2]}

def highlight(a):
    ExtAPI.SelectionManager.NewSelection(a)

def getMeshData(ns, mesh):
    elementIds = []
    for geoId in ns.Location.Ids:
        elementIds.extend(mesh.MeshRegionById(geoId).ElementIds)
    elementIds = list(set(elementIds))
    elements = [mesh.ElementById(elementId) for elementId in elementIds]
    centroids = np.asarray([list(element.Centroid) for element in elements], dtype=float)

    return elements, centroids

def getElementAroundCoords(meshData, coords, r, plane="xy"):
    elements, centroids = meshData
    coords = np.asarray(coords)
    axes = axeDict[plane]
    diffs = centroids[:, axes] - coords[axes]
    distSq = np.sum(diffs**2, axis=1)
    filter = distSq <= r*r
    return [e for e, tof in zip(elements, filter) if tof]

def findMatchingFaces(element, goalVector):
    goalVec = np.asarray(goalVector, dtype=float)
    goalVec = goalVec/np.linalg.norm(goalVec)
    cNodes = element.CornerNodes
    cNodeIds = element.CornerNodeIds
    matches = []
    if element.Type in [ElementTypeEnum.kTri3, ElementTypeEnum.kQuad4, ElementTypeEnum.kTet4]:
        return [1]
    hexFaces = eTypeToFaceIndex[element.Type]
    for I, nodeIndices in enumerate(hexFaces):
        p0 = np.array([cNodes[nodeIndices[0]].X, cNodes[nodeIndices[0]].Y, cNodes[nodeIndices[0]].Z])
        p1 = np.array([cNodes[nodeIndices[1]].X, cNodes[nodeIndices[1]].Y, cNodes[nodeIndices[1]].Z])
        p2 = np.array([cNodes[nodeIndices[2]].X, cNodes[nodeIndices[2]].Y, cNodes[nodeIndices[2]].Z])
        normVec = np.cross(p1-p0, p2-p0)
        normVec = normVec/np.linalg.norm(normVec)
        dotProduct = np.dot(normVec, goalVec)
        if abs(dotProduct-1) < 1e-3:
            matches.append(I)
    return matches

def elesToFaces(eles, targetFaceVec):
    actualIds = [x.Id for x in eles]
    faceIndices = []
    for x in eles:
        faceIndice = findMatchingFaces(x, targetFaceVec)
        faceIndices.append(faceIndice[0])
    return actualIds, faceIndices

def cfs(eles, targetFaceVec):
    elementIds, faceIndices = elesToFaces(eles, targetFaceVec)
    faceSel = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.MeshElementFaces)
    faceSel.Ids = elementIds
    faceSel.ElementFaceIndices = faceIndices
    return faceSel

def getFaceSelectionAtCoords(meshData, coords, r, targetFaceVec, plane="xy"):
    elements = getElementAroundCoords(meshData, coords, r, plane=plane)
    return cfs(elements, targetFaceVec)

def setHeatFlow(heatFlow, times, heats):
    heatFlow.Magnitude.Inputs[0].DiscreteValues = [Quantity(time, "s") for time in times]
    heatFlow.Magnitude.Output.DiscreteValues = [Quantity(heat, "W") for heat in heats]

globals().update(locals())

analysis = Model.Analyses[0]
meshData = getMeshData(Model.NamedSelections.Children[0], analysis.MeshData)

nSteps = 50
deltaT = 0.1
Tfinal = nSteps*deltaT

settings = analysis.AnalysisSettings
settings.NumberOfSteps = 1
settings.CurrentStepNumber = 1
settings.StepEndTime = Quantity(Tfinal, "s")

timeSteps = np.linspace(0,Tfinal,nSteps+1)
timeStepList = timeSteps.tolist()
R = 0.07
theta_total = np.pi           # arc to sweep [rad]
dthdt = theta_total / Tfinal    # angular rate [rad/s]
theta0 = 0.0                    # starting angle [rad]
theta = theta0 + dthdt*timeSteps
xcoords = R*np.cos(theta)a
ycoords = R*np.sin(theta)
Rspot = 0.003

for x in range(nSteps):
    faceSel = getFaceSelectionAtCoords(meshData, [xcoords[x],ycoords[x],0], Rspot, [0, 0, 1])
    coords = coords + [0.0002, 0, 0]
    heatFlow = analysis.AddHeatFlow()
    heatFlow.Name = "Custom Heat Flow " + str(x)
    heatFlow.Location = faceSel
    heatValues = []
    for j in range(nSteps+1):
        if j == x+1:
            heatValues.append(2)
        else:
            heatValues.append(0)
    #print(heatValues)
    setHeatFlow(heatFlow, timeSteps, heatValues)

title: Selecting Mesh Faces in ANSYS Mechanical
text:
Selecting Mesh Faces by Position and Normal in ANSYS Mechanical
Selecting elements and element faces is a very powerful tool when it comes to applying various conditions in ANSYS. This page is entirely dedicated to the selection of elements and their faces.
The reason this is so difficult is because while the elements themselves are objects, the faces are abrbitrarily indexed starting from 0. This means that for the exact same setup, the 0th face of a cubic element could be in opposite directions between models. Additionally, there are no normal vectors or centroids provided for these faces, despite them being one of the strongest ways to apply loads during analysis. Using a singular function getFaceSelectionAtCoords() now allows us to get a highly accurate circle of elements and the faces on their surface.



Elements


The math behind the code can be found at the end of this page!
import numpy as np

eTypeToFaceIndex = {
    ElementTypeEnum.kTri3: [[0, 1, 2]],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTri6: [[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6]],
    ElementTypeEnum.kQuad4: [[0, 1, 2, 4]],
    ElementTypeEnum.kQuad8: [[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTet4: [
        [0, 1, 3], [1, 2, 3], [2, 0, 3], [0, 2, 1]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kTet10: [
        [0, 1, 3, 4, 8, 7],
        [1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 8],
        [2, 0, 3, 6, 7, 9],
        [0, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kPyramid5: [
        [0, 3, 2, 1], [0, 1, 4], [1, 2, 4], [3, 4, 2], [0, 4, 3]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kPyramid13: [
        [0, 3, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6, 5],
        [0, 1, 4, 5, 10, 9],
        [1, 2, 4, 6, 11, 10],
        [3, 4, 2, 12, 11, 7],
        [0, 4, 3, 9, 12, 8]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kWedge6: [
        [0, 2, 1], [3, 4, 5], [0, 1, 4, 3],
        [1, 2, 5, 4], [0, 3, 5, 2]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kWedge15: [
        [0, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6],
        [3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11],
        [0, 1, 4, 3, 6, 13, 9, 12],
        [1, 2, 5, 4, 7, 14, 10, 13],
        [0, 3, 5, 2, 12, 11, 14, 8]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kHex8: [
        [0, 1, 5, 4], [1, 2, 6, 5], [2, 3, 7, 6],
        [3, 0, 4, 7], [0, 3, 2, 1], [4, 5, 6, 7]
    ],
    ElementTypeEnum.kHex20: [
        [0, 1, 5, 4, 8, 17, 12, 16],
        [1, 2, 6, 5, 9, 18, 13, 17],
        [2, 3, 7, 6, 10, 19, 14, 18],
        [3, 0, 4, 7, 11, 16, 15, 19],
        [0, 3, 2, 1, 11, 10, 9, 8],
        [4, 5, 6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15]
    ]
}

axeDict = {"xy": [0, 1], "xz": [0, 2], "yz": [1, 2]}


def highlight(selection):
    ExtAPI.SelectionManager.NewSelection(selection)


def getMeshData(ns, mesh):
    elementIds = []
    for geoId in ns.Location.Ids:
        elementIds.extend(mesh.MeshRegionById(geoId).ElementIds)

    elementIds = list(set(elementIds))
    elements = [mesh.ElementById(elementId) for elementId in elementIds]
    centroids = np.asarray(
        [list(element.Centroid) for element in elements],
        dtype=float
    )
    return elements, centroids


def getElementAroundCoords(meshData, coords, r, plane="xy"):
    elements, centroids = meshData
    coords = np.asarray(coords, dtype=float)
    axes = axeDict[plane]
    diffs = centroids[:, axes] - coords[axes]
    distSq = np.sum(diffs**2, axis=1)
    keep = distSq <= r**2
    return [element for element, include in zip(elements, keep) if include]


def findMatchingFaces(element, goalVector):
    goalVec = np.asarray(goalVector, dtype=float)
    goalLength = np.linalg.norm(goalVec)
    if goalLength == 0:
        raise ValueError("targetFaceVector cannot be zero")
    goalVec = goalVec / goalLength
    cornerNodes = element.CornerNodes
    matches = []

    for faceIndex, nodeIndices in enumerate(eTypeToFaceIndex[element.Type]):
        p0 = np.array([
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[0]].X,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[0]].Y,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[0]].Z
        ])
        p1 = np.array([
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[1]].X,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[1]].Y,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[1]].Z
        ])
        p2 = np.array([
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[2]].X,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[2]].Y,
            cornerNodes[nodeIndices[2]].Z
        ])

        normal = np.cross(p1 - p0, p2 - p0)
        normalLength = np.linalg.norm(normal)
        if normalLength == 0:
            continue
        normal = normal / normalLength
        if abs(np.dot(normal, goalVec) - 1) < 1e-3:
            matches.append(faceIndex)

    return matches


def elementsToFaces(elements, targetFaceVector):
    elementIds = []
    faceIndices = []

    for element in elements:
        matches = findMatchingFaces(element, targetFaceVector)
        if matches:
            elementIds.append(element.Id)
            faceIndices.append(matches[0])

    return elementIds, faceIndices


def createFaceSelection(elements, targetFaceVector):
    elementIds, faceIndices = elementsToFaces(elements, targetFaceVector)
    faceSelection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(
        SelectionTypeEnum.MeshElementFaces
    )
    faceSelection.Ids = elementIds
    faceSelection.ElementFaceIndices = faceIndices
    return faceSelection


def getFaceSelectionAtCoords(
    meshData, coords, r, targetFaceVector, plane="xy"
):
    elements = getElementAroundCoords(meshData, coords, r, plane)
    return createFaceSelection(elements, targetFaceVector)


Math behind the code
For an xy search, an element with centroid \(\mathbf{c}\) is obtained when
\[
(c_x-q_x)^2+(c_y-q_y)^2 \le r^2,
\]
where \(\mathbf{q}\) is the search center and \(r\) is the radius. Ignoring the third coordinate makes this a cylindrical search through the mesh rather than a spherical one.
Each element type has a different local face definition, so eTypeToFaceIndex maps every face to its local node indices. For the first three corner positions \(\mathbf{p}_0\), \(\mathbf{p}_1\), and \(\mathbf{p}_2\), the unit normal is
\[
\hat{\mathbf{n}}=
\frac{(\mathbf{p}_1-\mathbf{p}_0)\times(\mathbf{p}_2-\mathbf{p}_0)}
{\left\|(\mathbf{p}_1-\mathbf{p}_0)\times(\mathbf{p}_2-\mathbf{p}_0)\right\|}
\]
The node order matters because reversing it reverses the normal. The face matches a target direction \(\hat{\mathbf{g}}\) when
\[
\left|\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{g}}-1\right|<10^{-3}.
\]
Because the test is near (+1), it accepts faces pointing with the target vector, not against it. The tolerance corresponds to roughly (2.6^). The resulting element IDs and local face numbers can be assigned directly to a MeshElementFaces selection.
The final loop advances the search center in (x), creates one heat-flow object at each location, and gives each object a 2000 W peak at its matching time point. Mechanical interpolates between the tabular values, so additional points are needed if a square pulse is required.

title: An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
text:
An Object-Oriented Python Wrapper for FEMM
Finite Element Method Magnetics (FEMM) has a python scripting interface thats commands are procedural, meaning you establish an instance and then edit its attributes line by line before moving onto a seperate instance. This is useable for small scale projects but becomes unreadable and bulky fast. To overcome this, I wrote a small python femm wrapper to automate simulations for a paper I was part of.
By organizing pyFEMM into objects, it becomes significantly easier to construct larger scale models.

Ex 1



A model with a pair of permanent magnets positioned below a pentagon shaped iron. Force + energy per body is calculated.


from pyFemmStructs import Model
import numpy as np

magWidth = 12
magHeight = 6
yc = 5

mod1 = Model(depth=50, symmetric=False) # radius is no longer used here
steel = mod1.loadMaterial("1018 Steel")
N52 = mod1.loadMaterial("N52")
air = mod1.loadMaterial("Air")

airOuter = mod1.addBlock(air,'circle', [0,0,60])
magnet1 = mod1.addBlock(N52, 'rectangle center', [-magWidth*0.6,yc,magWidth,magHeight],90)
magnet2 = mod1.addBlock(N52, 'rectangle center', [magWidth*0.6,yc,magWidth,magHeight],-90)
iron = mod1.addBlock(steel,'coordlist',[-1.2*magWidth,10, -1.2*magWidth,15, 0,20, 1.2*magWidth,15, 1.2*magWidth,10 ])
mod1.drawAll()
mod1.solve()
print(iron.getForce())
foo = mod1.getEnergyTable()
print(foo)


Ex 2



Axisymmetric model with vertically poled magnet partially within a coil. Force is computed between the two.


from pyFemmStructs import Model
import numpy as np

model1 = Model(symmetric=True) 
N52Linear = model1.createMaterial('N52Linear', 1.05, 1.05, 1109e3)
air = model1.loadMaterial("Air")
cu = model1.loadMaterial("Copper")
airOuter = model1.addBlock(air,'half circle', [80])
magnet = model1.addBlock(N52Linear, 'rectangle corners', [0,0,10,20],90)
circuit1 = model1.addCircuit('circuit1',5,1)
coil1 = model1.addCoil(circuit1,cu, [12,-10,16,10],100,shape='rectangle corners')
model1.drawAll()
model1.solve()
print(coil1.getForce())


The wrapper
One important nuance is that as of now the region must be large enough with respect to the objects to simulate a flux moving to infinity. In the future I hope to implement a boundary condition to allow simulation towards infinity.
import femm
import numpy as np

class Model:
    def __init__(self, depth=1, symmetric=False):
        self.symmetric = symmetric
        self.blocks = []
        self.materials = []
        self.coils = []
        self.circuits = []
        
        femm.openfemm() 
        femm.newdocument(0)
        
        if symmetric:
            femm.mi_probdef(0, 'millimeters', 'axi', 1e-8, 0, 30)
        else:
            femm.mi_probdef(0, 'millimeters', 'planar', 1e-8, depth, 30)
        
    def addBlock(self, material, shape, coords, direction = 0, controlPoint = None, meshSize = None):
        block = Block(self, str(material), shape, coords, direction, controlPoint, meshSize)
        self.blocks.append(block)
        return block
    
    def addCoil(self, circuit, material, coords, turns, shape='rectangle',
                direction=0, controlPoint=None, meshSize=None):
        coil = Coil(self, str(circuit), str(material), coords, turns, shape,
                    direction, controlPoint, meshSize)
        self.coils.append(coil)
        return coil

    def addCircuit(self, circuitName, amps, isSeries=1 ):  
        circuit = Circuit(self,circuitName,amps,isSeries)
        self.circuits.append(circuit)
        return circuit
    
    def drawAll(self):
        for x in self.blocks:
            x.draw()
        for x in self.coils:
            x.draw()
            
    def solve(self):
        femm.mi_saveas('blah.fem')
        femm.mi_analyze()
        femm.mi_loadsolution()
                  
    def getEnergyTable(self):
        Energy = []
        for x in self.blocks:
            Energy.append(x.getEnergy())
        return np.array(Energy)
                          
    def createMaterial(self, matName, ux, uy, hC=0, j=0, cDuct=0, lamD=0, phiHMax=0, lam=0, phiHx=0, phiHy=0, nstr=0, dwire=0):
        material = Material(matName, ux, uy, hC, j, cDuct, lamD, phiHMax, lam, phiHx, phiHy, nstr, dwire, True)
        return material
    
    def loadMaterial(self, matName):
        material = Material(matName)
        return material
    
    def getForceOnBlocks(self,blockList):

            theBlock.selectBlock()
        # horizontal force, vertical force
        return(femm.mo_blockintegral(18),femm.mo_blockintegral(19))
        
    
class Block:
    def __init__(self, model, material, shape, coords = None, direction = 0, controlPoint = None, meshSize = None):
        self.model = model
        self.shape = shape
        self.material = material
        self.direction = direction
        self.coords = coords
        self.circuit = '<None>'
        self.turns = 0
        if controlPoint is not None:
            self.x = controlPoint[0]
            self.y = controlPoint[1]
            self.autoCenter = False
        else:
            self.autoCenter = True
        if meshSize is not None:
            self.autoMesh = 0
            self.meshSize = meshSize
        else:
            self.autoMesh = 1
            self.meshSize = 0
        
    def getForce(self):
        # this method only works for blocks abutting free space
        femm.mo_clearblock()
        femm.mo_selectblock(self.x, self.y)
        # horizontal force, vertical force
        return(femm.mo_blockintegral(18),femm.mo_blockintegral(19))
    
    def selectBlock(self):
        femm.mo_selectblock(self.x,self.y)
    
    def getEnergy(self):
        femm.mo_clearblock()
        femm.mo_selectblock(self.x, self.y)
        # energy, co-energy
        return(femm.mo_blockintegral(2), femm.mo_blockintegral(17))
    
    def setCoords(self, coords):
        self.coords = coords
    
    def draw(self):
        print(self.shape,self.material)
        if (self.shape == 'coordlist'):
            coords = self.coords
            if len(self.coords)%2 == 0:
                for i in range(0, len(coords), 2): 
                    femm.mi_drawline(coords[i], coords[i+1], coords[(i+2)%len(coords)], coords[(i+3)%len(coords)])
            xMax, yMax = max(coords[::2]), max(coords[1::2])
            xMin, yMin = min(coords[::2]), min(coords[1::2])
            if self.autoCenter:
                self.x,self.y = xMin+0.5*(xMax-xMin), yMin+0.5*(yMax-yMin)
        elif (self.shape == 'circle'):
            # coords: centerx, centery, radius
            centerx,centery,radius = self.coords[0],self.coords[1],self.coords[2]
            femm.mi_drawarc(centerx,centery+radius,centerx,centery-radius, 180, 30)            
            femm.mi_drawarc(centerx,centery-radius,centerx,centery+radius, 180, 30)
            if self.autoCenter:
                self.x,self.y = centerx,centery+0.95*radius
        elif (self.shape == 'half circle'):
            # coords: [radius]; centered at origin, spans -90 to 90 deg, closed along the axis
            r = self.coords[0]
            femm.mi_drawarc(0, -r, 0, r, 180, 1)
            femm.mi_drawline(0, r, 0, -r)
            if self.autoCenter:
                self.x, self.y = 0.025*r, 0.95*r
        elif self.shape in ('rectangle','rectangle center'):
            # coords: centerx, centery, width, height
            centerx,centery,width,height = self.coords[0],self.coords[1],self.coords[2],self.coords[3]
            femm.mi_drawrectangle(centerx-width/2,centery-height/2,centerx+width/2,centery+height/2)
            if self.autoCenter:
                self.x,self.y = centerx+0.49*width,centery+0.49*height
        elif (self.shape == 'rectangle corners'):
            # coords: x1, y1, x2, y2
            femm.mi_drawrectangle(self.coords[0],self.coords[1],self.coords[2],self.coords[3])
            if self.autoCenter:
                width = (self.coords[2]-self.coords[0])
                height = (self.coords[3]-self.coords[1])                
                self.x,self.y = self.coords[0]+0.98*width,self.coords[1]+0.98*height  
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown shape '{self.shape}'")
            
        femm.mi_addblocklabel(self.x, self.y)
        femm.mi_selectlabel(self.x, self.y)
        femm.mi_setblockprop(self.material, self.autoMesh, self.meshSize, self.circuit, self.direction, 0, self.turns)
        femm.mi_clearselected()
        
class Material:
    def __init__(self, matName=None, ux=None, uy=None, hC=None, j=None, cDuct=None, lamD=None, phiHMax=None, lam=None, phiHx=None, phiHy=None, nstr=None, dwire=None, create = False):
        self.matName = matName
        if create:
            femm.mi_addmaterial(matName, ux, uy, hC, j, cDuct, lamD, phiHMax, lam, phiHx, phiHy, nstr, dwire)
        else:
            femm.mi_getmaterial(matName)
            
    def __str__(self):
        return self.matName
    
class Circuit:
    def __init__(self, model,circuitName, amperes, isSeries):
        self.amps = amperes
        self.isSeries = isSeries
        self.circuitName = circuitName
        femm.mi_addcircprop(circuitName, self.amps, self.isSeries)
    def __str__(self):
        return self.circuitName
    
class Coil(Block):
    def __init__(self, model, circuit, material, coords, turns, shape='rectangle',
                 direction=0, controlPoint=None, meshSize=None):
        super().__init__(model, material, shape, coords, direction, controlPoint, meshSize)
        self.circuit = circuit
        self.turns = turns

title: Checking Units
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation: Checking Units
One of the most tedious parts of automation in ANSYS is unit inconsistency. Rather than having to double check everything, I usually just use the below script as a mechanical snippet (the code is run every solve).
In a case where the same script is used across multiple projects, consider placing a unit checker at the top of your code.
# Accepted units: "m", "cm", "mm", or "um"
unit = "mm"

unitSystems = {
    "m": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardMKS,
    "cm": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardCGS,
    "mm": MechanicalUnitSystem.StandardNMM,

title: Setting Thermal Conductivity as a Function of Gap in APDL
text:
When analyzing heat transfer in ANSYS, there is often times a need to consider thermal conductivity accounting for the conductivity of air despite it being so small. In this case, the bar and cube (10 mm x 10 mm x 20 mm and 10 mm x 10 mm x 10mm) are steel and held at 23 and 22 degrees respectively. Across a small gap, the conduction is not negligible, but may not be treated as if they were touching.



Bar and cube 13.8 micrometers apart


k_air = 0.026 ! thermal conductivity of air near room temp (W/m-K)
h_max = 5e4  ! full contact thermal contact conductance (W/m^2-K)
g_max = 5e-3 ! max gap over which to construct the table (m)
n_tcc = 60 ! number of points to include in the table

g_cap = k_air/h_max ! this is the gap below which to hold at g_max

*del,tcc_tab,,nopr
*dim,tcc_tab,table,n_tcc+1,1,1,GAP

! Open gap is negative: rows run from -g_max up to -g_cap
*do,i,1,n_tcc
    ! power-law spacing of gap entries in the tabke
    g = g_max*(g_cap/g_max)**((i-1)/(n_tcc-1)) 
    tcc_tab(i,0) = -g  ! gap is negative in ansys convension
    tcc_tab(i,1) = k_air/g  ! contact conductivity W/m^2-K 
*enddo

tcc_tab(n_tcc+1,0) = 1.0  ! ansys positive gap is actually pushed together
tcc_tab(n_tcc+1,1) = h_max  ! saturate at max contact conductivity

rmodif,cid,14,%tcc_tab%
nldiag,cont,on

The tcc table is set up so that at smaller values, the steps are closer together as any function depending on an inverse asymptotically approaches zero as the independant variable increases.

The presentation combines analytical magnetic circuits, 2D field calculations, 3D FEA comparisons, and a physical cylindrical-magnet experiment. The experiment’s 2D prediction is about 11 N; the measured plateau is roughly 10 N by visual reading. The reported hysteresis loop is about 60 mN, less than 1%. Page 3 lists gravity compensation (reduced energy consumption and actuator size), vibration isolation including quasi-zero-stiffness springs, and non-contact operation relevant to wear, friction, and cleanliness. Normal configurations change separation across facing surfaces; shear configurations change overlap through relative motion along the interacting surfaces. Torsional springs and actuators incorporating gravity compensation are also discussed. Variations include arrays, iron, ironless designs, and Halbach arrangements.
Modeling approaches: analytical magnet-pair formulas; equivalent magnetic charge or current; Fourier harmonic models; lumped magnetic circuits; 2D FEA (FEMM is identified by the presentation as free/open source); 3D FEA; and semi-analytical combinations.
Magnetic circuit analogy: reluctance corresponds to resistance, magnetomotive force (MMF) to voltage, and magnetic flux to current. Equivalent-charge/current illustration credited to Lahdo et al. 2017.



The figures contrast air/vacuum’s linear B-H response, soft iron’s nonlinear hysteresis loop, and a permanent magnet’s remanence and demagnetization curve. The magnet’s approximately linear recoil relation is:
B = B_r + mu*H
mu_r = mu/mu_0
For air/vacuum, B = mu_0*H. For a general linear medium the relation is B = mu*H; the slide’s air/vacuum equation should not be generalized to every material. Page 7 shades magnetic energy areas on the B-H diagrams. These areas represent energy density (J/m^3), distinct from E_i (J/m).



Magnetic behavior depends on shape. A sourced illustration from www.mriquestions.com compares demagnetization factors for cylinders, plates, ellipsoids, a cube, and a sphere. A separate plot shows rectangular-section E_0/E* increasing from approximately 0.50 to 0.77 as w/t increases from 1 to 4 (visual readings, not tabulated data).
The slide prints B_0 = N B_ext but does not fully define the symbols or establish a general demagnetization law. Do not use that isolated expression as a universal design formula; the reliable takeaway here is shape dependence.



The rectangular magnet is poled across thickness t and moves axially into the tube. For a sufficiently long magnet and tube, the field can be approximated using three cross-sectional regions: empty tube, magnet inside tube, and magnet outside tube. The diagrams show magnetic-circuit and 2D field representations.
Define each E as magnetic energy per unit thickness of an axial slice. The approximate axial force magnitude for the indicated insertion direction is:
F ≈ E_0 - E_1
The circuit approximation for the air-gap flux density is:
B = B_r * (t/mu_r) / (t/mu_r + 2*g)
It treats the iron path as sufficiently permeable; saturated/thin iron requires a more complete calculation. E_0 can come from a handbook expression or 2D FEA. The normalization is:
E* = B_r^2 * t*w / (2*mu_r*mu_0)
The illustrated case gives E* = 101 J/m, E_1 = 0.09 E* = 9.1 J/m, and E_0 = 0.55 E* = 56 J/m. Their rounded difference is about 47 N, a derived estimate rather than an additional measurement.
Explanatory interpretation: if a displacement du replaces one slice with another, the energy changes by a quantity proportional to (E_0 - E_1)*du. Force follows from the change of energy with displacement. Do not insert an extra magnet length into the force equation: these E values are already per unit length.



Page 11 compares a nearly flat force estimate near F/E* ≈ 0.45 with a 3D FEA curve over insertion displacement. The numerical curve has entrance and exit effects. Agreement is best in the intermediate region; it is not uniform over all travel.
Page 12 shows that thinning the iron produces saturation and lowers the plateau (approximately 0.35 in the illustrated comparison). The same energy method can still be used, but E_1 should come from 2D FEA rather than the simple circuit formula. Field plots show localized high flux density.



For N52 magnets and 1018 steel in the studied rectangular configuration, a wall thickness about one-third of magnet width suffices. The graph plots F/E* against a/w for 2g/t = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3. The model represents periodic magnet configurations using spatial harmonics. The iron backing is idealized with permeability tending to infinity. Two scalar-potential regions satisfy Laplace’s equation, ∇²ψ = 0. The moving permanent magnet is represented by magnetic charge density:
sigma_m(y, y_r) = sum_{k=1..infinity} [a_k(y_r)*cos(p*k*y) + b_k(y_r)*sin(p*k*y)]
p = 2*pi/lambda_u

         = (mu_0*D_f*lambda_u/2) * sum_{k=1..infinity}
           a_k(y_r) * { [1-cosh(p*k*(z_2-z_s1))]*A_k
                        + sinh(p*k*(z_2-z_s1))*B_k }
                     / sinh(p*k*z_2)
This is a transcription, not an independently validated derivation. The slides do not fully define A_k, B_k, their boundary-condition calculation, or the magnetic-charge normalization. In particular, do not silently resolve unit conventions from the integral and expanded form without the underlying derivation. For a general blog, the harmonic concept and reported performance are more useful than presenting this as a ready-to-code solver.
The illustrated case labels a 20 mm period (lambda_pp on page 29), 5 mm magnet thicknesses, and a 0.5 mm gap. The plotted displacement response is approximately sinusoidal over 0-20 mm. Its vertical-axis labeling is not reliably readable, so do not quote an absolute force amplitude from it. The slide states that the first harmonic is accurate to within a few percent for the example; it does not establish this for every array.



The configuration is a coaxial pair magnetized along the axis. For tall magnets (t/R >> 1), the sticking/contact force approaches E* according to the slide. Reversing one magnet produces repulsion with nearly the same magnitude. The plot compares t/R = 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0; force decreases as separation increases.
The page does not restate the reference E* formula for this arrangement. The diagram labels R, while the axis uses u/r. Avoid building a numerical calculator from this slide without confirming radius and normalization conventions.



Three magnets with t/R = 0.5 form a push-pull arrangement: one interaction attracts while the other repels. The force-displacement curve is relatively flat near the middle of travel. The slide reports that small gaps and travels can attain F/E* ≈ 0.9. Plotted gap ratios are g/r = 0.2, 0.6, 1.0. The smallest gap yields the highest normalized force and a narrower available travel range. This is not a 90% energy efficiency claim.



The presentation concludes that E* provides an approximate upper-bound scale, changes in magnetic energy provide a useful route to force, and 2D FEA can exploit planar geometry and symmetry.
Listed next steps are design guidelines for stiffness and parasitic forces, misalignment, temperature variation, Halbach magnets, iron versus ironless designs, hysteresis estimates, and adding an actuator. These are future directions, not all completed results.

title: Passive Magnetic Springs: Source Reference for a Blog Post
text:
The presentation asks how to design useful passive magnetic springs with tractable formulas and modest computational effort before resorting to full 3D finite-element analysis (FEA). A central example is a long permanent magnet partly inserted into a soft magnetic tube. As overlap changes, cross-sectional regions with different magnetic energies replace one another. Their energy difference per unit length provides an approximate axial force.
This yields nearly constant force over a finite intermediate travel range. The force changes near the ends, and off-axis displacement can produce destabilizing lateral attraction. Iron improves force for a given magnet cross section but introduces saturation and hysteresis. Ironless layouts can recover comparable force by using larger magnets within a comparable overall envelope in the examples studied.
The presentation combines analytical magnetic circuits, 2D field calculations, 3D FEA comparisons, and a physical cylindrical-magnet experiment. The experiment’s 2D prediction is about 11 N; the measured plateau is roughly 10 N by visual reading. The reported hysteresis loop is about 60 mN, less than 1%. These are distinct observations, not a claim of less than 1% model error.

Page 1 contains the attribution above. Page 2 asks for useful design formulas addressing force, stiffness, travel, repeatability, low hysteresis, damping, parasitic forces and stiffness, temperature effects, and packaging. Design choices include magnet size, iron versus ironless constructions, Halbach arrangements, aspect ratio, and gap. A Linmot MagSpring product image illustrates an existing concept; it is not identified as the team’s prototype.
Page 3 lists gravity compensation (reduced energy consumption and actuator size), vibration isolation including quasi-zero-stiffness springs, and non-contact operation relevant to wear, friction, and cleanliness. Hysteresis and eddy currents remain possible damping mechanisms. Mechanical springs and pneumatics are alternatives.



Normal configurations change separation across facing surfaces; shear configurations change overlap through relative motion along the interacting surfaces. Torsional springs and actuators incorporating gravity compensation are also discussed. Variations include arrays, iron, ironless designs, and Halbach arrangements.
Modeling approaches: analytical magnet-pair formulas; equivalent magnetic charge or current; Fourier harmonic models; lumped magnetic circuits; 2D FEA (FEMM is identified by the presentation as free/open source); 3D FEA; and semi-analytical combinations.
Magnetic circuit analogy: reluctance corresponds to resistance, magnetomotive force (MMF) to voltage, and magnetic flux to current. Equivalent-charge/current illustration credited to Lahdo et al. 2017.



The figures contrast air/vacuum’s linear B-H response, soft iron’s nonlinear hysteresis loop, and a permanent magnet’s remanence and demagnetization curve. The magnet’s approximately linear recoil relation is:
B = B_r + mu*H
mu_r = mu/mu_0
For air/vacuum, B = mu_0*H. For a general linear medium the relation is B = mu*H; the slide’s air/vacuum equation should not be generalized to every material. Page 7 shades magnetic energy areas on the B-H diagrams. These areas represent energy density (J/m^3), distinct from E_i (J/m).



Magnetic behavior depends on shape. A sourced illustration from www.mriquestions.com compares demagnetization factors for cylinders, plates, ellipsoids, a cube, and a sphere. A separate plot shows rectangular-section E_0/E* increasing from approximately 0.50 to 0.77 as w/t increases from 1 to 4 (visual readings, not tabulated data).
The slide prints B_0 = N B_ext but does not fully define the symbols or establish a general demagnetization law. Do not use that isolated expression as a universal design formula; the reliable takeaway here is shape dependence.



The rectangular magnet is poled across thickness t and moves axially into the tube. For a sufficiently long magnet and tube, the field can be approximated using three cross-sectional regions: empty tube, magnet inside tube, and magnet outside tube. The diagrams show magnetic-circuit and 2D field representations.
Define each E as magnetic energy per unit thickness of an axial slice. The approximate axial force magnitude for the indicated insertion direction is:
F ≈ E_0 - E_1
The circuit approximation for the air-gap flux density is:
B = B_r * (t/mu_r) / (t/mu_r + 2*g)
It treats the iron path as sufficiently permeable; saturated/thin iron requires a more complete calculation. E_0 can come from a handbook expression or 2D FEA. The normalization is:
E* = B_r^2 * t*w / (2*mu_r*mu_0)
The illustrated case gives E* = 101 J/m, E_1 = 0.09 E* = 9.1 J/m, and E_0 = 0.55 E* = 56 J/m. Their rounded difference is about 47 N, a derived estimate rather than an additional measurement.
Explanatory interpretation: if a displacement du replaces one slice with another, the energy changes by a quantity proportional to (E_0 - E_1)*du. Force follows from the change of energy with displacement. Do not insert an extra magnet length into the force equation: these E values are already per unit length.



Page 11 compares a nearly flat force estimate near F/E* ≈ 0.45 with a 3D FEA curve over insertion displacement. The numerical curve has entrance and exit effects. Agreement is best in the intermediate region; it is not uniform over all travel.
Page 12 shows that thinning the iron produces saturation and lowers the plateau (approximately 0.35 in the illustrated comparison). The same energy method can still be used, but E_1 should come from 2D FEA rather than the simple circuit formula. Field plots show localized high flux density.



For N52 magnets and 1018 steel in the studied rectangular configuration, a wall thickness about one-third of magnet width suffices. The graph plots F/E* against a/w for 2g/t = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3. Force increases with wall thickness and approaches a plateau; larger gaps lower force. This is a configuration-specific rule of thumb.



Lateral displacement attracts the magnet toward the tube wall. Negative stiffness is much larger parallel to the poling direction than transverse to it in this example. The example specifies an N52 magnet, a 1018 tube, w = 12 mm, t = 10 mm, and a = 6 mm.
The left plot gives lateral force per millimeter of insertion versus lateral offset. The right plot gives lateral negative stiffness per millimeter of insertion versus 2g/t. Do not quote these normalized plot values as the total device force or stiffness. Larger gaps reduce the destabilizing stiffness. A useful blog explanation is that nearly constant axial force does not imply lateral self-centering.



Splitting the cross section into a moving central piece and stationary side pieces reduces moving mass. In the depicted geometry, the central piece has thickness t/2 and the side pieces t/4 each. The energy expression becomes:
F = E_0 - (E_1 - E_2)
E_2 accounts for the remaining stationary assembly’s cross section, as shown in the diagrams. Reported rounded examples:

The plots use dimensionless force F/E* and displacement u in millimeters. Page 27’s M3 curve illustrates a comparatively flat positive-force region. The slides do not provide a full optimized actuator design or control implementation.



The model represents periodic magnet configurations using spatial harmonics. The iron backing is idealized with permeability tending to infinity. Two scalar-potential regions satisfy Laplace’s equation, ∇²ψ = 0. The moving permanent magnet is represented by magnetic charge density:
sigma_m(y, y_r) = sum_{k=1..infinity} [a_k(y_r)*cos(p*k*y) + b_k(y_r)*sin(p*k*y)]
p = 2*pi/lambda_u

         = (mu_0*D_f*lambda_u/2) * sum_{k=1..infinity}
           a_k(y_r) * { [1-cosh(p*k*(z_2-z_s1))]*A_k
                        + sinh(p*k*(z_2-z_s1))*B_k }
                     / sinh(p*k*z_2)
This is a transcription, not an independently validated derivation. The slides do not fully define A_k, B_k, their boundary-condition calculation, or the magnetic-charge normalization. In particular, do not silently resolve unit conventions from the integral and expanded form without the underlying derivation. For a general blog, the harmonic concept and reported performance are more useful than presenting this as a ready-to-code solver.
The illustrated case labels a 20 mm period (lambda_pp on page 29), 5 mm magnet thicknesses, and a 0.5 mm gap. The plotted displacement response is approximately sinusoidal over 0-20 mm. Its vertical-axis labeling is not reliably readable, so do not quote an absolute force amplitude from it. The slide states that the first harmonic is accurate to within a few percent for the example; it does not establish this for every array.



The configuration is a coaxial pair magnetized along the axis. For tall magnets (t/R >> 1), the sticking/contact force approaches E* according to the slide. Reversing one magnet produces repulsion with nearly the same magnitude. The plot compares t/R = 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0; force decreases as separation increases.
The page does not restate the reference E* formula for this arrangement. The diagram labels R, while the axis uses u/r. Avoid building a numerical calculator from this slide without confirming radius and normalization conventions.



Three magnets with t/R = 0.5 form a push-pull arrangement: one interaction attracts while the other repels. The force-displacement curve is relatively flat near the middle of travel. ANSYS Mechanical Automation - Remote Point Pairs from Named Selections
For this project, I needed to represent a six-degree-of-freedom spring between tracks (stationary) and rollers (dynamic). This approach used pairs of remote points that had translational/rotational constraints and whose initial position was determined by the average between the centroids.
If more pairs were required, it would definetly be worthwhile to replace the hardcoded filtering and function sequence with a dictionary that could be looped through.
def avgOfCentroids(nsList):
    pts = []
    x = y = z = 0

    for ns in nsList:
        for id in ns.Location.Ids:
            pts.append(ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(id).Centroid)

    for p in pts:
        x += p[0]
        y += p[1]
        z += p[2]
    return x/len(pts), y/len(pts), z/len(pts)

def createRPs(nsList):
    coords = avgOfCentroids(nsList)
    for ns in nsList:

        c.YCoordinate = Quantity(coords[1], "m")
        c.ZCoordinate = Quantity(coords[2], "m")
        c.PilotNodeAPDLName = ns.Name

title: Automating 6DOF Bushing Contacts
text:
ANSYS Mechanical Automation: Creating 6DOF Bushing Contacts



Result of running script


When solving a mechanical model, points of contact can become extremely computationally demanding, requiring a heavily refined mesh around the contact region to determine local behavior. For some analyses, however, we do not require an accurate local representation and care more about the overall stiffness between two components.
In this case, we can simplify the expensive contact region with a 6 degree-of-freedom bushing joint, allowing us to represent the connection without the need for an extremely fine mesh.
The challenge to this approach is placing the bushing correctly. With the automation script I wrote below, all of the geometry difficulties are taken care of. The user must select 2 bodies (sphere + cylinder) and the script places a bushing contact lined up along the vector from the center of the sphere and cylinder.
(See end for notes about the code)
import numpy as np

_start_vars = set(dir())

def checkJ(cons):
    for x in cons:
        if "Joint" in str(x.ConnectionType):
            return x
    return None
    
def det3(M):
    return M[0][0]*(M[1][1]*M[2][2] - M[1][2]*M[2][1]) - M[0][1]*(M[1][0]*M[2][2] - M[1][2]*M[2][0]) + M[0][2]*(M[1][0]*M[2][1] - M[1][1]*M[2][0])

globals()['det3'] = det3

def solve_3x3(A, B):
    D = det3(A)
    Ax = [
        [B[0], A[0][1], A[0][2]],
        [B[1], A[1][1], A[1][2]],
        [B[2], A[2][1], A[2][2]]
    ]

    Ay = [
        [A[0][0], B[0], A[0][2]],
        [A[1][0], B[1], A[1][2]],
        [A[2][0], B[2], A[2][2]]
    ]

    Az = [
        [A[0][0], A[0][1], B[0]],
        [A[1][0], A[1][1], B[1]],
        [A[2][0], A[2][1], B[2]]
    ]

    return [det3(Ax)/D, det3(Ay)/D, det3(Az)/D]

globals()['solve_3x3'] = solve_3x3
    
def sphere_center(p1, p2, p3, p4):
    x1, y1, z1 = p1
    A = []
    B = []
    for x, y, z in [p2, p3, p4]:
        A.append([2*(x - x1), 2*(y - y1), 2*(z - z1)])
        B.append(x*x + y*y + z*z - x1*x1 - y1*y1 - z1*z1)

    return solve_3x3(A, B)



globals()['sphere_center'] = sphere_center

selected = list(ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CurrentSelection)

if "Sphere" in str(ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(selected[0]).SurfaceType):
    cylID = selected[1]
    sphereID = selected[0]
else:
    cylID = selected[0]
    sphereID = selected[1]

sph = ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(sphereID)
cyl = ExtAPI.DataModel.GeoData.GeoEntityById(cylID)

sphere = sph.Points
norms = cyl.Normals

norms = np.array(norms).reshape(-1, 3)
sphere = np.array(sphere).reshape(-1, 3)

p1 = norms[2]
p2 = norms[7]
p3 = norms[14]

A = np.vstack((p1, p2, p3))

eigenvalues, Vectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
D = np.diag(eigenvalues)

U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(norms, full_matrices=True)
S = np.zeros((norms.shape[0], norms.shape[1]))
np.fill_diagonal(S, s)

dirCyl = np.array(Vt[2])

cs = Model.CoordinateSystems
cs1 = cs.AddCoordinateSystem()

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [cylID]

cs1.OriginLocation = selection

sphereCenter = np.array(sphere_center(sphere[0], sphere[10], sphere[20], sphere[30]))

cs1.PrimaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveZAxis
cs1.PrimaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(dirCyl[0], dirCyl[1], dirCyl[2])

pointOnCylAxis = np.array([
    float(str(cs1.OriginX).split(" ")[0]),
    float(str(cs1.OriginY).split(" ")[0]),
    float(str(cs1.OriginZ).split(" ")[0])
])

OP = np.array(pointOnCylAxis-sphereCenter)

AtoC = np.cross(np.cross(OP, dirCyl), dirCyl)

AtoC = AtoC / np.linalg.norm(AtoC)

actual_point = sphereCenter + sph.Radius*AtoC

cs1.OriginX = Quantity(str(actual_point[0]) + " [m]")
cs1.OriginY = Quantity(str(actual_point[1]) + " [m]")
cs1.OriginZ = Quantity(str(actual_point[2]) + " [m]")

cs1.PrimaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveZAxis
cs1.PrimaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(AtoC)

cs1.SecondaryAxis = CoordinateSystemAxisType.PositiveXAxis
cs1.SecondaryAxisDirection = Vector3D(dirCyl)

cons = Model.Connections.Children

group = checkJ(cons)

if checkJ(cons) is None:
    group = Model.Connections.AddConnectionGroup()

group.ConnectionType = AutoDetectionType.Joint

joint = group.AddJoint()
joint.Type = JointType.Bushing

rp1 = Model.RemotePoints.AddRemotePoint()
rp2 = Model.RemotePoints.AddRemotePoint()

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [cylID]

rp1.Location = selection

selection = ExtAPI.SelectionManager.CreateSelectionInfo(SelectionTypeEnum.GeometryEntities)
selection.Ids = [sphereID]

rp2.Location = selection

joint.ReferenceLocation = rp1
joint.MobileLocation = rp2

rp1.CoordinateSystem = cs2
rp2.CoordinateSystem = cs2
To see the actual math behind this: (INSERT HERE)
When it came to finding the center of the sphere, I recycled it from one of my older scripts before found out how to use CPython (numpy) in ansys mechanical so there are multiple technically not needed functions above that do smaller scale matrix operations.
Because CPython is still technically in beta, there are many weird bugs when it comes to compiling these scripts. In this code specifically, I had to force various functions to be considered global so I could access them at all using globals()['sphere_center'] = sphere_center.
If this code were to be used for a large amount of connections, I would recommend writing a function which sorts your selections into pairs based on centroid proximity and looping through these pairs with the above code.

title: Designing Passive Magnetic Springs with Energy-Based Models
text:
Overview
A vertical actuator under load should not have to be supplying energy given that a passive spring is handling this static load. The actuator should be left to handle disturbances and changes in motion. While conventional springs accomplish this, their force varies with displacement; a magnetic spring, however, may provide a constant, contactless force over a range of travel.
By looking at the difference in energy between two bodies, one inside a tube and one outside, we may estimate force. From this estimation, a design model can be made before performing analysis on it using FEMM, then finally performing a physical experiment.

The design problem
One priority in this model was a force-displacement relationship that under load and gravity would remain relatively unchanged. One way to accomplish this is a long permanent magnet that slides through a tube. The magnet is polarized across its cross section, perpendicular to its direction of motion. (EXPLAIN MORE WHY THIS IS A GOOD SOLUTION)






Figure 1: A long magnet entering a tube shown divided into two-dimensional cross-sectional regions. The plots are analytical and simulation tools, not measurements.



Given a long enough tube, it can be shown as a cross section without regarding the end behaviors.


Theory
Let (E_0) be magnetic energy per unit length (of the magnet outside the tube), and let (E_1) be the energy per unit length (of the magnet inside the tube). Both have units of joules per meter.
As the magnet moves forward by du, a slice of the cross section changes to match the inside state. Therefore, axial force can be represented by
\[
F \approx E_0-E_1.
\]
THe total energy can be written as a sum of the regions. So icnreasing the overlap between the two magnets transfers eneergy from the outside region to the inside region. We can then diffrentiate energy with respect to displacement to get the difference. Because its energy per unit length, there is no need for magnet length to be considered.
For the rectangular tube model, the air-gap flux density is approximated with a magnetic circuit:
\[
B = B_r\frac{t/\mu_r}{t/\mu_r+2g},
\]
where (B_r) is the magnet remanence, (t) is its dimension along the poling direction, (g) is the one-sided air gap, and (mu_r) is the magnet recoil relative permeability. This relation assumes that the iron provides a sufficiently permeable return path.
Normalizing by the reference energy per length now gives
\[
E^*=\frac{B_r^2tw}{2\mu_r\mu_0},
\]
where (w) is the other cross-sectional dimension and (mu_0) is the permeability of free space.


Considering the entrance and exit
The cross-sectional estimate has no entrance or exit, so it predicts a constant force. A 3D model restores those end effects.






Figure 2: The dotted line is the energy-based estimate; the solid curve is 3D FEA. Agreement is strongest after entry and before the far end of the tube.



In this simulated curve, force spikes as the magnet enters the tube, then flattens out once inside the device, then drops as the magnet approaches the exit of the tube. In the case of the iron, if the wall has enough mass to remain below saturation, a magnetic circuit may provide an estimate of the energies. In the case where the iron saturates, the energy on the inside increases which throws off the relationship we seek.


Iron vs ironless design
Soft iron concentrates flux which increases force for a given set up but also introduces saturation and hysteresis. An ironless design would remove the hysteretic complications but would require more magnetic material to produce the same force.






Figure 3: Equal-force packaging comparison. In this geometry, the iron design reaches about (0.45E^), while the three-magnet ironless arrangement reaches about (0.15E^) for the same magnet-area normalization.



For the comparison shown above, the iron design produces 3x more force given the same amount of magnetic material. Because E scales with cross sectional area, this corresponds to a factor of (sqrt{3}).
This is a tradeoff and the choice would come down to whether the priority is compactness or precision.


The experiment
The physical test used a diametrically poled N52 cylindrical magnet: its magnetization points across the diameter rather than along its axis. The magnet was 6.35 mm in diameter and 25.4 mm long. It moved into a 25 mm-long 1018-steel tube with a 7 mm inner diameter and a 16 mm outer diameter.
For a circular magnet of diameter (d)
\[
E^*=\frac{\pi d^2B_r^2}{8\mu_r\mu_0}, \qquad \frac{E_0}{E^*}=\frac{1}{2},
\]
and obtains (E_1/E^) from 2D FEMM analysis. The reference scale for the test magnet is (E^ ). The diameters imply a radial clearance of 0.325 mm.






Figure 4: The apparatus and its force comparison. Blue is measurement, orange is 3D FEA, and the dotted yellow line is the constant 2D estimate.





Lateral stability issue
The tube attracts an off-center magnet toward the nearest wall. That is a negative lateral stiffness: a small radial displacement produces a force that increases the displacement instead of restoring the magnet to center.






Figure 5: Two-dimensional FEA of the cylindrical case shows lateral attraction and predicts lower negative stiffness as the radial gap increases. The plotted quantities are normalized per millimeter of insertion.



In the circular example, the same attraction for offsets parallel and transverse to the poling direction. Increasing the air gap reduced this destabilizing stiffness, but also reduced axial force. Bearings, flexures, or another guidance mechanism must therefore guide the lateral load. A nearly flat axial force curve may not be interpreted as self-centering behavior.

title: Automating Temperature Assignments in ANSYS
text:
Automating Temperature Assignments in ANSYS Mechanical with Python
When working with thermal models in ANSYS, assigning temperature boundary conditions to components can be time consuming, especially when these conditions are coming from an external source.
For multiple analyses, I needed to apply temperature changes to components using data from a text file, so rather than manually creating and scoping the respectibe geometry, I used regexp and python to automate the process.
In the case below, the data naming convention used sensor names such as NTC01 or RTD02, to apply a different naming convention simply edit the regexp search.
import re

a = DataModel.GetObjectsByName("Geometry")[0].Children
b = Model.NamedSelections
d = DataModel.GetObjectById(266)

def getRow(file, T):
    finalRow = None
    var = float("inf")
    
    with open(file, 'r') as f:
        next(f)
        for line in f:
            iRow = line.strip().split(',')
            initial = float(iRow[0])
            diff = abs(T-initial)
            if diff < var:
                var = diff
                finalRow = iRow
    f.close()
    return finalRow

def checkEnd(s):
    result = re.search(r'NTC\d+$', s) or re.search(r'RTD\d+$', s) 
    return result

T2 = 12
T1 = 0

ntc2 = getRow(r'FILENAME', T2)
ntc1 = getRow(r'FILENAME', T1)

rtd2 = getRow(r'FILENAME', T2)
rtd1 = getRow(r'FILENAME', T1)

for x in a:
    for y in a.Children:
        if checkEnd(y.Name):
            num = int(y.Name[-2:])
            temp = d.AddTemperature()
            temp.Name = y.Name[-5:]
            if y.Name[-5:-2] == 'NTC':
                print y.Name
                temp.Magnitude.Output.SetDiscreteValue(0, Quantity(float(ntc2[num]) -float(ntc1[num]), "C"))
            else:
                print y.Name
                temp.Magnitude.Output.SetDiscreteValue(0, Quantity(float(rtd2[num]) -float(rtd1[num]), "C"))

            temp.PromoteToNamedSelection()
            
            nsList = DataModel.GetObjectsByName("Named Selections")[0].Children
            
            for x in nsList:
                if x.Name == y.Name[-5:]:
                    c = x
                    break

            c.ScopingMethod = GeometryDefineByType.Worksheet
            c.GenerationCriteria.Add(None)
            c.GenerationCriteria[0].EntityType = SelectionType.GeoBody
            c.GenerationCriteria[0].Criterion = SelectionCriterionType.Name
            c.GenerationCriteria[0].Operator = SelectionOperatorType.Equal
            c.GenerationCriteria[0].Value = y.Name
            c.Generate()
